title: Show me your glory (Exodus 33:12–23)
hook: Moses in the cleft of the rock sees only God's back as he passes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the molten calf, made of earrings while Moses was late coming down. Your line was impatience makes idols. What did your hand reach for while you waited? Day three hundred ninety-eight.

Have you ever walked into a room just after someone left it? The chair is still warm. A coat still swings on its hook. The air still smells a little like them. You missed them by a minute, but the room still tells you who was here. After the calf, after the broken tablets, Moses has been pleading for his people. And then he asks for something bold. Not for a sign. Not for a plan. In the King James Bible: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory."
screen: `A WARM CHAIR, A SWINGING COAT.` → `AFTER THE CALF, MOSES PLEADS.` → `SHEW ME THY GLORY.`

segments.voice: God says yes, and no. Yes: I will make all my goodness pass before you, and I'll proclaim my name. But no: "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." So God makes a plan, tender and almost playful. There is a place by me, he says, on a rock. I'll put you in a cleft of the rock, and cover you with my hand while I pass by. Then I'll take my hand away, "and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen." Moses gets to see where God has just been. The glory he asked for is kavod in Hebrew. Lexicons link it to a root meaning heavy, so some readers hear glory as weight: what makes God weighty, real, present. And Moses can only bear it from behind, after it's passed. Readers notice a puzzle here. Just a few verses earlier the same chapter says God spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. So which is it? Some interpreters say the first means closeness, the way friends talk, and the second means the full sight of God, which no one could bear. The text keeps both, side by side. Gregory of Nyssa, a Greek bishop and writer, read it as a picture of following God: you see God's back because you are walking behind him. And the Gospel of John holds both sides too: of Jesus, "we beheld his glory," and a few verses on, "No man hath seen God at any time." Some Christians say faith is often like this: not seeing God's face, but noticing, a little late, that someone was just here.
screen: `YES, AND NO.` · `A CLEFT IN THE ROCK, A HAND.` · `KAVOD: GLORY THAT HAS WEIGHT.` · `YOU SEE HIS BACK BY FOLLOWING.` · then, large: `THOU SHALT SEE MY BACK PARTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for where God has just been. Or, if that language isn't yours, where goodness has just passed. Settle, and breathe. Go back over the last day or two, slowly, like walking back through rooms. Was there a moment that turned out kinder than you expected? A conversation that went right? A worry that quietly didn't happen? A stranger's help? Don't rush to explain it. Just notice the warm chair. If you pray, you can say thank you for what passed by. The bell holds the time.
Kavod. Hebrew for glory, linked to a root meaning heavy: what Moses asked to see, and saw only as God's back, passing by.
Your line: his back, passing by. Tonight, before you sleep, name one place where something good passed through your day, even if you only noticed afterward. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this passage when talking about knowing God in hindsight, and some spiritual traditions, like the daily examen, look back over the day for where God was present.

fork.setup: you're Moses. you've just asked to see God's glory, and God says no one can see his face and live. what happens next?
options: you're sent back down the mountain.
God hides you in a rock and passes by.
God shows you a vision in a dream.
fork.reveal: God puts Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and lets him see his back as he passes. a no that turns into a gentler yes.

original.note: Hebrew: glory, honor. Lexicons link it to a root meaning heavy.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses asked for a light show.
what it means: he asked to see God, and was allowed to see where God had just been.
what a scholar hears: kavod, which lexicons link to the root for heavy; and a chapter that keeps 'face to face' and 'thou canst not see my face' side by side.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's half-finished coffee replaced (it echoed day 387's 'coffee still warm on the counter'); cut 'the boldest thing anyone asks in the whole book of Exodus', 'Moses' boldest prayer', 'worn out and afraid' (not in the text), 'Christian writers have loved this scene', 'in the fourth century', 'many interpreters' and 'for many people, this is what faith often feels like'; kavod-as-weight framed as a lexicon link some readers hear, and the etymology myth item replaced with one from the text; John 1:14 and 1:18 were cited in reverse order and are now quoted exactly (KJV).
Kavod from the root k-b-d, 'to be heavy': standard lexicon (BDB). Confirm.
Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Moses (c. 390), book II, reads seeing God's back as following God; paraphrased. Confirm the date and the summary.
